Part 0 — The Model and the Method

Everything the paper takes for granted before its first result: how DINOv2 turns an image into 261 vectors, why one looks for concepts rather than neurons, and how a sparse autoencoder produces the 32,000-concept dictionary.

After this page you can
  • describe what a DINOv2 ViT-B/14 with registers computes: 261 tokens of dimension 768, attention heads, residual stream, LayerNorm, MLP;
  • write one attention head as a weighted average of value vectors, and say why this is the formula used in §7 of the paper;
  • explain how DINOv2 is trained (DINO, iBOT, KoLeo) and what a "frozen features + linear probe" evaluation is;
  • say why neurons are not the unit of interpretation (polysemanticity, superposition) and state the linear representation hypothesis in words;
  • write A≈ZD with the constraint that defines k-means, PCA, NMF, archetypal analysis and sparse autoencoders, and read a sparse code;
  • explain the TopK and BatchTopK rules and the archetypal constraint D=SC used for the paper's dictionary;
  • use the DinoVision demo and read a concept heat map or a feature visualisation.

Before you start#

The paper (§1–2) states in a few lines what this page unfolds: a model (DINOv2), a hypothesis (linear representation), a tool (an archetypal sparse autoencoder) and a way to look at the result (heat maps, visualisations). Nothing on this page is a result of the paper; it is the setting of all of them.

How to read this page#

Sections 1–2 describe the network. Section 3 explains why one looks for concepts. Section 4 explains how they are extracted. Section 5 shows how to look at them. Facts about other papers were checked against their primary sources; where the paper is the only source, the text says "according to the paper". Every number not in the paper is computed by checks/check_01.py.

The story of the page in six steps#

  1. Tokens. An image becomes a sequence of 261 vectors of dimension 768 (§1).
  2. Layers. Each block adds an attention update and an MLP update to every token; the sum is the residual stream (§1.3).
  3. Training. DINOv2 learns by self-distillation; its features are used frozen, with linear probes (§2).
  4. Concepts. Neurons mix many things; a representation can hold more features than dimensions if they are sparse (§3).
  5. Dictionary. Factorise the activations as A≈ZD with sparse Z; the paper uses an archetypal SAE (§4).
  6. Looking. Heat maps, visualisations, and the DinoVision demo (§5).

What you need#

Linear algebra, softmax, and what a neural network is. The mathematics used later (coherence, convex hulls, PCA) is recalled on page 2.

1. Vision transformers#

A ViT cuts the image into patches, turns each patch into a vector (a token), and repeatedly lets tokens exchange information (attention) and transform themselves (MLP), each time by adding an update to the token. The paper analyses the final token vectors of DINOv2.

1.1 From pixels to 261 tokens#

Problem. A transformer takes a sequence of vectors, an image is a grid of pixels. The solution is to cut the grid into square patches and treat each patch as a word.

In the paper §2 · p. 5 and App. K · p. 52

"A pretrained Vision Transformer f:X→Rt×d": any image x yields activations a=f(x)∈Rt×d, "i.e. t token embeddings of dimension d". "We used DINOv2-B with 4 registers as f, with d=768, t=261." The tokens are "256 spatial patches arranged in a 16×16 grid plus one classification token and four register tokens."

  1. 224/14=16 patches per side, so 162=256 patch tokens.patch size 14 for DINOv2 ViT-B/14.
  2. Each patch (14×14×3 = 588 numbers) is multiplied by a learned matrix to give a vector of dimension d=768.this is the patch embedding.
  3. A learned position embedding is added to each patch token.without it the network could not tell where a patch comes from; page 4 studies this position signal.
  4. One class token (cls) and four register tokens are added, giving t=256+1+4=261.they have no pixels; they are learned vectors that can store global information (§1.4).

The result is a matrix X∈R261×768: 200,448 numbers per image and per layer. "Activations of a layer" means this matrix at that depth. In the paper's row convention one token activation is a row a∈R768.

1.2 Attention: a weighted average of values#

Problem. Tokens must exchange information; a patch of fur needs to know there is a rabbit elsewhere. Attention lets each token read the others.

A head of ViT-B has three learned matrices WQ​,WK​,WV​∈R768×64. For the token matrix X:

QV​=XWQ​,K=XWK​,=XWV​(261×64 each).​

Token i is the query, token j offers a key (what it is) and a value (what it gives). The output of the head is

YYi​αi​​=softmax(64​QK⊤​)V=AV,=j=1∑261​αij​Vj​,=softmax(Qi​K⊤/8)∈Δ261.​
Qi​Kj⊤​
score: how much token i wants token j (a dot product of two 64-dimensional vectors).
/64​=/8
keeps the scores of order one, so the softmax does not saturate.
softmax (per row)
turns the 261 scores into non-negative weights αij​ that sum to 1.
Yi​
a weighted average of the value vectors: a point inside their convex hull. This is exactly what §7 of the paper uses (page 5). Here A is the attention matrix, not the activations.
Reminder — softmax

softmax(s)j​=esj​/∑l​esl​: all weights are strictly positive and sum to 1, so the output is never on the boundary of the hull of the values. Dividing the scores by a small temperature makes the weights concentrate on the largest score. more

Worked example — three tokens

Scores (2,1,0) give weights (0.665,0.245,0.090). With 2-D values (3,0), (0,3), (−3,−3) the output is 0.665(3,0)+0.245(0,3)+0.090(−3,−3)=(1.726,0.464), inside the triangle of the three values.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: raise one score: its weight tends to 1 and the output slides to that value. Lower the temperature: same effect. Put all scores equal: the output is the plain mean of the five values. The output never leaves the dashed polygon.

Multi-head. A block has H=12 heads of dimension 64 (12×64=768). Each head has its own WQ(h)​,WK(h)​,WV(h)​. The outputs are concatenated and projected back to 768 dimensions with WO​; equivalently the update is a sum over heads of WO(h)​ applied to the head output, ∑h​WO(h)​Y(h). This sum is what leads to Minkowski sums on page 5.

Pitfall — the values depend on the image

The values Vj​=WV​LN(xj​) are computed from the tokens of the current image. The convex hull of values is rebuilt for every image. Our reading, page 6.

1.3 The block and the residual stream#

Problem. A deep network must stay trainable and each layer should refine, not replace, what exists. The answer is the residual connection: a layer outputs an update that is added to its input.

x′x′′​=x+γ1​⊙Attn(LN(x)),=x′+γ2​⊙MLP(LN(x′)).​
LN
LayerNorm: for each token separately, subtract the mean of its 768 coordinates, divide by their standard deviation, then apply a learned scale and shift. "Pre-norm" means it is applied before the branch, not after.
Attn
multi-head attention (§1.2): the only place where tokens interact.
MLP
two linear layers with a GELU in between, 768→3072→768, applied to each token alone.
γ1​,γ2​
LayerScale: a learned per-coordinate multiplier, initialised very small, that eases training of deep networks. DINOv2 uses it (initial value 10−5 in the official configuration).

After 12 blocks a token is x12​=x0​+∑l​(attentionl​+MLPl​): the residual stream is a running sum of updates. A final LayerNorm is applied to the output of the last block; the paper writes a=f(x), the output of the network f; whether this is before or after this final LayerNorm matters for the geometry (our reading, page 6).

How many numbers are in the attention matrix of one head for one image?

Answer

261×261=68,121, one weight per (query, key) pair; each row sums to 1.

1.4 Registers#

Problem. Darcet et al. (2023, arXiv:2309.16588) observed that large ViTs produce "high-norm tokens appearing during inference primarily in low-informative background areas of images": the network recycles some patch tokens to store global information, which corrupts feature maps. Their fix is to "provide additional tokens to the input sequence". These extra tokens, the registers, are never read as an output; they are free memory slots that attention can use. The paper uses the DINOv2 model with four registers (the abstract of Darcet et al. does not give the number; four is the paper's choice of model).

Why it matters here §4 · p. 9, App. K · p. 52

Registers give the dictionary a place to find concepts that are about the whole image: the paper finds concepts that fire only on register tokens and capture "global scene properties like illumination and motion blur" (page 3).

2. DINOv2 and its evaluation#

DINOv2 is trained without labels: a student network must reproduce the output of a slowly-moving teacher on different views of the same image, at the image level (DINO) and at the masked-patch level (iBOT), with a regulariser (KoLeo) that spreads features out. Its frozen features are then read by simple linear probes.

The paper does not train anything: it takes DINOv2 as given. This section gives the training objectives because §6 of the paper ("Toward interpolative geometry") appeals to them, and to explain why a linear probe on the output is meaningful.

2.1 DINO: self-distillation without labels#

Problem. Learn features of images without labels. DINO (Caron et al. 2021, arXiv:2104.14294) uses self-distillation: two networks with the same architecture, a student and a teacher. The teacher's weights are an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student's: θt​←mθt​+(1−m)θs​ with m close to 1. Only the student receives gradients.

  1. From one image, draw several crops: 2 global (large, 224 px) and several local (small, 96 px).in the official DINOv2 configuration: 2 global crops with scale 0.32–1, 8 local crops with scale 0.05–0.32.
  2. The teacher processes the global crops only; the student processes all crops.forces "local to global" consistency: a small piece must predict what the whole shows.
  3. Each network ends with a head (an MLP then a layer of prototypes: learned vectors p1​,…,pK​). The head outputs K scores, one per prototype, and a softmax turns them into a distribution p over prototypes.a soft, learned clustering of the image into K pseudo-classes.
  4. The loss is the cross-entropy −∑k​pkteacher​logpkstudent​ between the teacher's and the student's distributions.the student imitates the teacher; no label is involved.
  5. The teacher output is centred (a running mean is subtracted) and sharpened by a low temperature.centring prevents one prototype from dominating, sharpening prevents the uniform solution; together they prevent collapse (Caron et al.). DINOv2 uses centring (the official configuration offers Sinkhorn–Knopp as an option).
In the paper §6 · p. 16, footnote

"The global DINO head matches teacher representations using 128k prototypes, while the iBOT head performs masked prediction with its own 128k prototype vocabulary." The footnote: a DINO head "consisting of a 4096→4096→256 MLP that outputs scores over 128k prototypes", and an iBOT head with the same shape. "Both heads apply softmax normalization to produce probability distributions over their respective prototype vocabularies, effectively implementing implicit clustering with soft assignments."

Fact check against the official configuration

The file dinov2/configs/ssl_default_config.yaml of the official repository gives, for the DINO head, 65,536 prototypes, a bottleneck of 256, a hidden width of 2048 and 3 layers; the iBOT head has the same values and separate_head: false (it shares the DINO head). KoLeo weight 0.1, mask probability 0.5. This default file does not show the paper's 128k prototypes and 4096 width; the released checkpoints were possibly trained with other settings (the DINOv2 paper discusses 131,072 prototypes). We could not confirm the paper's footnote (two heads, 128k prototypes, 4096→4096→256) from the official files: read it as "according to the paper". Only the general idea (soft assignments to a large set of prototypes) matters for the paper's argument.

2.2 iBOT: the same idea on masked patches#

DINO compares whole-image outputs. iBOT (Zhou et al. 2021, arXiv:2111.07832) adds a patch-level task: some patch tokens of the student's input are masked (replaced by a learned mask token); the student must output, for each masked patch, the same prototype distribution as the teacher gives for the unmasked patch. The loss is again a cross-entropy between softmaxes, now summed over masked patches. This forces patch tokens to carry local semantic content, which is why DINOv2 patch tokens are good for segmentation and depth. In DINOv2 each token of the masked crops has its own prototype head output (the paper says the iBOT head has "its own 128k prototype vocabulary"; the official default shares head parameters, see the check above).

2.3 KoLeo: spreading the features out#

The Kozachenko–Leonenko (KoLeo) regulariser (Sablayrolles et al. 2018) is a differential-entropy estimator. For a batch of n normalised feature vectors xi​ it is −n1​∑i​log(minj=i​∥xi​−xj​∥): it is large when some point has a very close neighbour. Minimising it pushes each vector away from its nearest neighbour, so features fill the sphere uniformly instead of clumping. DINOv2 adds it with weight 0.1 (official configuration). The paper cites it as "encouraging entropy maximization, promoting uniform distribution across the representation space while avoiding collapse" (§6 · p. 16).

Our reading — what the training facts do and do not say

The paper uses prototype heads and KoLeo to suggest that tokens are "mixtures of prototypes". The heads act on the network's output through a softmax; they say nothing yet about the geometry of the 768-dimensional token itself. See page 6.

2.4 Frozen features and linear probes#

Problem. How to judge a representation learned without labels? Freeze the network and train only a linear probe: a matrix W∈Ro×d mapping a feature (a token or a pooled vector) to o outputs: class scores, a per-pixel class, a depth value. If a linear map suffices, the information is linearly accessible. DINOv2 is trained on a large automatically curated image set rather than uncurated data (Oquab et al. 2023, arXiv:2304.07193), and is meant to give features that work "across image distributions and tasks without finetuning".

The paper uses three probes on the output tokens (Fig. 2 · p. 3):

  • classification on ImageNet-1k: a linear head on the concatenation of the class token and the mean of the patch tokens (App. B.2 of the paper);
  • segmentation on ADE20K: a linear map from each patch token to a class;
  • depth estimation on NYU Depth v2: a linear map from each patch token to a depth value.

A probe is linear, so its output on the codes is Y=AW⊤=Z(DW⊤): the key identity of page 3.

Pitfall — probes show access, not use

A probe reads information the network keeps; it does not prove that the network uses it. The paper's "task-relevant" concepts are defined through the probe, i.e. relative to a linear read-out.

3. Interpretability: from neurons to concepts#

One wants to know what a representation contains. Single neurons are a poor unit because each fires for several unrelated things; the likely reason is superposition, where more features than dimensions are stored as nearly orthogonal directions. The linear representation hypothesis packages this into a model that a dictionary can be fitted to.

3.1 "Where" versus "what"#

Attribution methods (saliency, gradient × input, RISE, toolbox) answer where: which pixels or tokens a prediction depends on. They do not say what the model sees there. Concept-based methods answer what: they find directions of the activation space that stand for human-readable notions (fur, shadow, "left side"). The paper does both: concepts give the "what", importance scores and RISE maps give the "where" (page 3).

Why not read concepts off single neurons (coordinates)? A coordinate of the 768-dimensional token is a neuron-like unit. The paper's §2 states the empirical finding: features "behave as nearly orthogonal directions, active only in restricted contexts, while neurons themselves are polysemantic". A neuron is polysemantic when it responds to several unrelated features. This motivates two conclusions: "(i) neurons are not the appropriate locus of interpretability, and (ii) one must recover the latent basis along which the model effectively operates."

3.2 Superposition#

Problem. A d-dimensional space has only d orthogonal directions, yet a model must represent far more features (objects, textures, positions). Elhage et al. (2022, Toy Models of Superposition) show in toy networks that when features are sparse (rarely active at the same time) a model stores more features than dimensions, in superposition: each feature gets a direction, and the directions are not orthogonal. The paper cites this as "a recurring phenomenology of large models".

Worked example — interference

Take d=2, atoms d1​=(1,0), d2​=(−21​,23​​), d3​=(−21​,−23​​), so di​⋅dj​=−21​.

  • Only feature 1 active, a=d1​: read-outs (1,−21​,−21​). The true code is (1,0,0); the others read −21​ (interference).
  • Features 1 and 2 active, a=d1​+d2​=(21​,23​​): read-outs (21​,21​,−1). The true code is (1,1,0): both active features read 21​ instead of 1.

Interference is the price; sparsity is what makes it affordable: with 5 features each active with probability 0.1 independently, two or more are active together only 8.1% of the time. Smaller maxi=j​∣di​⋅dj​∣ (the coherence) means less interference; this is why the paper asks for quasi-orthogonality and recalls optimal packings (toolbox).

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: with c=2 equal to d, read-outs are exact. With c=3,4,5,6, activate one feature and see the others read non-zero values; activate two and see the active ones distorted. The coherence printed below grows with c in the plane: you cannot pack many nearly orthogonal directions into two dimensions, which is why real models have d=768 and c≫d.

3.3 The linear representation hypothesis#

Linear Representation Hypothesis Def. 1 · §2 · p. 5

A representation a∈Rd satisfies the LRH if a=zD with a dictionary D∈Rc×d and coefficients z∈Rc such that (i) c≫d (overcomplete), (ii) μ(D)=maxi=j​∣Di​Dj⊤​∣≤ε with unit rows (quasi-orthogonal), (iii) ∣supp(z)∣≤k≪c (sparse).

In words: a representation is a sparse sum of a few nearly orthogonal feature directions drawn from a large list. This is the toy of §3.2 made precise. The formal statement, its three conditions decoded and its geometric motivation (Tammes, Thomson, spherical codes, Grassmannian frames) are on page 3. The hypothesis is useful because it can be turned into an inverse problem: if it holds, finding the concepts means finding D, which is the subject of §4.

The paper adopts the LRH "as a working baseline"; its later parts study what that baseline misses (page 4).

4. Dictionary learning and sparse autoencoders#

Given a matrix of activations A, find sparse codes Z and a dictionary D with A≈ZD. The classical methods differ by the constraint they put on Z and D; sparse autoencoders learn Z with an encoder; the paper uses a stable variant whose atoms are convex combinations of data.

4.1 A family of factorisations#

Problem. Under the LRH, concepts are the rows of an unknown D. Many methods fit a factorisation; they differ in the constraint, hence in what a concept is.

From LRH to dictionary learning App. B · p. 33
(Z⋆,D⋆)=Z,Dargmin​ ∥A−ZD∥F2​

  • Each panel shows the same green points. Blue dots are atoms that are points (centres, archetypes); orange arrows are atoms that are directions.

4.2 Sparse autoencoders#

Problem. With n in the hundreds of millions of tokens and c=32,000, classical optimisation is slow and gives no function to apply to a new activation. A sparse autoencoder (SAE; Cunningham et al. 2023, Bricken et al. 2023) learns an encoder that maps an activation to its sparse code in one pass.

zL​=Ψθ​(a),a^=zD,=∥a−zD∥22​ (+λ∥z∥1​ for ReLU).​
Ψθ​
one linear layer followed by a non-linearity that makes most outputs exactly 0.
zD=∑i​zi​Di​
reconstruction as a combination of the atoms that fire.

Reading a code. If zi​=2.3 on token t, concept i "fires on token t with strength 2.3", and token t's activation contains 2.3Di​. Over a heat map, one colours each of the 256 patches by zi​ (§5.1). Quality of the reconstruction is measured by R2=1−∥A−ZD∥F2​/​A−Aˉ​F2​, and the fraction of variance unexplained is FVU=1−R2. The paper's dictionary has R2>88%, i.e. FVU<0.12.

4.3 How sparsity is enforced: ReLU+L1, TopK, BatchTopK#

  • ReLU + L1. z=max(0,aWe​+b) and a penalty λ∥z∥1​ in the loss. Sparsity is indirect, tuned by λ, and the L1 penalty shrinks the codes (a bias).
  • TopK. Keep the k largest pre-activations of each token, set the others to 0. Exactly k active codes per token; no penalty; no shrinkage.
  • BatchTopK (Bussmann et al. 2024). Keep the k⋅B largest pre-activations in a batch of B tokens, over the whole batch. The average is still k per token, but a complicated token may use more and a simple one fewer.

The paper writes: "Codes Z are produced via a single-layer encoder with BatchTopK projection" with k=8 (§2 · p. 5). The toy below uses 3 tokens and 5 concepts.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: with ReLU every positive entry survives. With TopK, k=2, every row keeps exactly two entries (token 2 keeps two tiny ones). With BatchTopK the same six survivors are chosen over all tokens: token 2 keeps none, token 3 keeps four. Check the printed counts per token.

Worked example (the default matrix)

Rows (2,−0.5,1,0.3,0.9), (0.2,0.1,−0.3,0.4,0), (3,1.5,0.8,2.2,1.9). Top-2 per token keeps {2,1}, {0.4,0.2}, {3,2.2}. BatchTopK with k=2 keeps the 6 largest positive entries of all: 3,2.2,2,1.9,1.5,1, i.e. 2, 0 and 4 codes per token.

4.4 The archetypal SAE used in the paper#

Problem. Plain SAEs are unstable: two runs from different seeds give different dictionaries, which undermines any conclusion drawn from "the" concepts (the paper cites Paulo et al. 2025 and Papadimitriou et al. 2025). Archetypal SAEs (Fel et al. 2025, arXiv:2502.12892) anchor each atom geometrically: atoms must lie in the convex hull of the data, which the authors report "significantly enhances the stability" of the dictionary; a "mildly relaxed" version (RA-SAE) is the one that matches state-of-the-art reconstruction. The DinoVision demo says its concepts come from an RA-SAE.

The paper's configuration §2 · p. 5
Z,Dmin​ s.t.  ​∥A−ZD∥F2​Z≥0, ∥Zi​∥0​≤k, Di​∈conv(A).​

"We set c=32,000 atoms and k=8 active codes per token, approximate conv(A) by 128,000 centroids extracted via k-means over 1.4M ImageNet-1K images (with augmentation), and parametrize D=SC with S row-stochastic. Codes Z are produced via a single-layer encoder with BatchTopK projection. Training with Adam for 50 epochs yields R2>88%."

C∈R128000×768
fixed: centroids of k-means on the activations; a cheap stand-in for the convex hull of all tokens.
S∈R32000×128000
learned; each row is ≥0 and sums to 1 (row-stochastic), so row i of SC is a convex combination of centroids.
D=SC
atom i is in conv(centroids)⊂conv(A) (the centroids are averages of data, so are inside the hull).
Z≥0, ∥Zi​∥0​≤8
concept strengths are non-negative: a concept is present or absent, not "negative".
Reminder — convex hull

conv(P) is the set of all convex combinations (non-negative weights summing to 1) of points of P. A point of the hull is never outside the range of the data. more

Why it matters. Atoms in the hull are in-distribution (they look like real activations) and reproducible. Three consequences for the rest of the guide: atoms are not forced to be orthogonal, the code Z≥0 only adds, and an atom is "an average of real activations" (the paper's page 4 and 5 arguments build on this). Counting: S has 32,000×128,000≈4.1×109 entries, against 2.5×107 for a free D; the training set has 1.4M×261≈3.65×108 tokens per epoch (our arithmetic).

Our reading — a dictionary is one fit among many

The concepts come from one training run of one method; a different c, k or constraint gives other atoms. The paper's statements about "the" dictionary are statements about this one. See page 6.

5. Seeing a concept#

A concept is a vector; to look at it one shows the images and tokens where it fires (heat maps) and an image synthesised to excite it (feature visualisation). The DinoVision demo packages both for the 32,000 concepts.

5.1 Top-activating images and heat maps#

For concept i, run many images, keep those with the largest maxt​Zt,i​ (top-activating images), and colour each of the 256 patches by Zt,i​ (a heat map; red means a large code). The class and register tokens are shown separately: they have no position in the image. Heat maps tell where the concept fires.

Pitfall — where it fires is not what it is about

In a ViT a token's value depends on all tokens through attention, so a concept can fire off the object it depends on. The paper's "Elsewhere" concepts show this (page 3).

5.2 Feature visualisation#

Visualisation App. K · p. 52

"For concept visualization we use Feature Accentuation (FA) from Hamblin et al. 2024: we start from maximally activating images of each concept and perform 1024 steps of gradient ascent optimization parameterized in Fourier space with MACO (Fel et al. 2023) constraints on the magnitude of the spectrum, boosted according to natural image statistics approximately following 1/ω2 where ω represents cycles per image."

gradient ascent
change the image pixels to increase the concept's code zi​ (the output of model + SAE for atom i).
Fourier parametrisation
the image is described by its spectrum, so that optimisation acts on frequencies, which gives smoother pictures than pixel-wise optimisation.
MACO
keeps the magnitude of the spectrum fixed to that of natural images and optimises only the phase, which prevents high-frequency artefacts.
1/ω2 boost
natural images have power spectra falling roughly as 1/ω2; the magnitude is scaled that way.
Feature Accentuation
start from a real top-activating image rather than noise, so that the result stays close to a real image: it accentuates what the concept responds to in it.

These are the pictures of tile 3 and tile 4 of Fig. 1. They are an aid: an optimised image shows what excites the concept, not everything it means.

5.3 The DinoVision demo#

How to read this figure
  • Each point is one concept (atom); its position is a UMAP projection, "where spatial proximity indicates conceptual similarity", with a caution that global clustering patterns should be read with care (UMAP). Its size reflects how often it fires.
  • Clicking a point shows the activation pattern on the 261-token grid (256 patches, one class, four registers): redder means a stronger code, next to the feature visualisation.
  • Controls (paper caption and the site): point size and heatmap opacity; co-occurrence links between concepts that often fire together; direct entry of a concept id; exploring a neighbourhood (radius); image size and an "energy" slider on the site.
  • Not shown: the concept's importance for a task; the demo's interface is a map of one dictionary.

The demo is at kempnerinstitute.github.io/dinovision. It opens with a content-warning gate; read it and accept it to enter. Use it to find the concepts the paper mentions: register-only concepts for illumination and motion blur, position concepts "left", "right", "bottom".

6. Summary and reflexes#

The setting in ten lines
  1. DINOv2 ViT-B/14 with 4 registers turns a 224×224 image into t=261 tokens of dimension d=768 (256 patches + cls + 4 registers).
  2. One attention head outputs Yi​=∑j​αij​Vj​, a weighted average of values; 12 heads of dimension 64 add up through WO​.
  3. A block adds an attention update and an MLP update to the residual stream, each after LayerNorm (pre-norm), with LayerScale.
  4. DINOv2 is trained by self-distillation (DINO + iBOT) with a KoLeo regulariser; features are used frozen with linear probes.
  5. Neurons are polysemantic; features are stored in superposition as nearly orthogonal directions.
  6. LRH: a=zD, c≫d, small coherence, sparse z.
  7. Dictionary learning: A≈ZD; k-means, PCA, NMF, AA, SAE differ by constraint.
  8. SAE: encoder + TopK/BatchTopK; quality is R2.
  9. Archetypal SAE: D=SC, atoms in the convex hull of 128,000 centroids; c=32,000, k=8, 1.4M images, 50 epochs, R2>88%.
  10. Heat maps show where, feature visualisation shows an exciting image; DinoVision gives both.
  • When you see softmax(⋅)V → a point of the convex hull of the values.
  • When you see "a concept fires here" → ask whether that says where the concept depends on.
  • When you see A≈ZD → rows of D are concepts, rows of Z say which fire on each token.
  • When you see an SAE → ask which sparsity rule, which constraint on D, which R2.
  • When you see an external fact about DINOv2 → check whether it is from the paper or from the DINOv2 files.

Next: page 3 states the hypothesis formally and scores the concepts against three tasks.

7. Exercises#

Exercise 1 — Count the tokens ★

An image of 448×448 pixels is fed to a ViT with 14×14 patches and 4 registers. How many tokens? How many attention weights in one head?

Hint

Patches per side, then add the special tokens.

Solution

448/14=32, so 1024 patches; plus 1 + 4: t=1029. The attention matrix is 10292=1,058,841 per head. (The paper uses 224 px: t=261.)

Exercise 2 — One attention step ★

A head has scores (0,ln2,ln4) for three keys with scalar values (10,20,30). Compute the weights and the output.

Hint

es=(1,2,4).

Solution

Weights (1,2,4)/7; output (10+40+120)/7=170/7≈24.29, inside [10,30].

Exercise 3 — Residual stream ★★

In a pre-norm block, write the final token after L blocks as a sum, and explain why an update γ⊙Attn(⋅) with γ≈0 leaves the token almost unchanged.

Hint

Unroll x←x+update.

Solution

xL​=x0​+∑l=1L​(γ1,l​⊙Attnl​+γ2,l​⊙MLPl​) (before the final LayerNorm). If γ≈0, the branch adds almost nothing, so the block is nearly the identity: this is why LayerScale with a tiny initial value (here 10−5) makes deep networks easy to start.

Exercise 4 — Interference ★★

Take the three unit vectors of the superposition example (pairwise inner product −21​). Feature 1 has strength 2 and feature 2 strength 1. Compute a and the three read-outs di​⋅a. Why is a threshold at 0 not enough to recover the support?

Hint

ri​=∑j​zj​di​⋅dj​ with Gram matrix G=23​I−21​11⊤.

Solution

r1​=2−21​=1.5, r2​=1−1=0, r3​=d3​⋅(2d1​+d2​)=−1−21​=−1.5. Feature 2 is active (strength 1) but reads 0: the interference from feature 1 cancels it exactly, and a threshold at 0 would miss it. Sparse coding with a proper solver (not a one-shot read-out) is needed.

Exercise 5 — TopK versus BatchTopK ★★

Two tokens have positive pre-activations (5,4,1,0.5) and (0.3,0.2,0.1,0.1). Which codes survive with TopK k=2 and with BatchTopK k=2? Which rule gives a better reconstruction of the first token and why?

Hint

BatchTopK keeps the k×2=4 largest of all eight numbers.

Solution

TopK: (5,4,0,0) and (0.3,0.2,0,0). BatchTopK: the four largest are 5,4,1,0.5, all in token 1; token 2 keeps nothing. The first token keeps four codes, so its reconstruction is better; the second is sacrificed because it carries little energy. The budget follows the tokens that need it.

Exercise 6 — Which constraint? ★★

For each statement name the method of App. B: (a) every code row is a canonical basis vector; (b) atoms are orthonormal; (c) atoms are convex combinations of data points and codes are on the simplex; (d) all entries of both factors are non-negative. For (c), what does the paper's archetypal SAE change?

Solution

(a) k-means (ACE); (b) PCA (ICE); (c) archetypal analysis; (d) NMF (CRAFT). The archetypal SAE keeps the constraint on atoms (D=SC, row-stochastic S, 128,000 centroids) but replaces the simplex constraint on codes by Z≥0 and ∥Zi​∥0​≤8 (BatchTopK, produced by an encoder).

Exercise 7 — Reconstruction quality ★★

An SAE has R2=0.88. What is the fraction of variance unexplained? If ​A−Aˉ​F2​=100, what is ∥A−ZD∥F2​? Is 88 % "high"? What does R2 not tell you?

Solution

FVU =0.12; the residual is 12. Whether this is high depends on the baseline (k-means or PCA with the same budget). R2 measures energy, not which directions are lost: a concept carrying little variance can be unreconstructed.

Exercise 8 — Parameter count of the archetypal constraint ★★★

Compare the number of free parameters of D (free) and of S in D=SC, with c=32,000, d=768, 128,000 centroids. Why is the second more expensive, and what does the archetypal SAE gain?

Hint

C is fixed, only S is learned.

Solution

Free D: 32,000×768=2.46×107. S: 32,000×128,000=4.1×109 entries (minus the row-sum constraints), about 167 times more. The cost buys a guarantee: every atom is a convex combination of centroids of real activations, hence inside the data's hull and stable. In practice rows of S can be parametrised by a softmax and stay manageable on a GPU; we have not checked the authors' implementation.
